Well, I don't know if maybe just this one pocket of people got
confused, or if everyone is confused (not likely), but here goes.

If vampire A is bleeding at +1 Stealth (due to Kine Domination for
example) can vampire B (controlled by the victim methusulah) play a
deflection without generating +1 intercept? We've always played that
in order to react to a vampire's actions either by blocking or playing
a different reaction card, you had to catch them doing it. The logic
being that stealth represents your hiding what you're doing from
sight, if they can't see you, how can they react at all to what you're
doing.

Second question, if you have a directed bleed card, can you nominate
someone besides your prey as the target? We've always played that the
built in bleed has to go to your prey, but a directed bleed can go to
any methusulah. Otherwise, what is the card difference between a
directed attack (say Ambush, which doesn't specify that it has to be
your prey, just that it can't be your own minion) and a Computer
Hacking, which doesn't say that it has to be directed at your prey
either?

Sorry if these are stupid questions, but we've played with these as
our interpretations for many years, and Norman gave us a wake up call,
so now we're waking up, and like normal, we're a little bearish about
it. My apologies to Norman if I was rude or seemed that way, but I
tend to be that way at times. Sorry for that, but those changes make
significant changes in the ways that our deck design and concepts
work.

Thanks in advance.

Lee

Messages.Body:
In article <39dbe8ac....@news.ionet.net>,
lf...@ionet.net (Lee Fent) wrote:

> If vampire A is bleeding at +1 Stealth (due to Kine Domination for
> example) can vampire B (controlled by the victim methusulah) play a
> deflection without generating +1 intercept?

Yes. This is the best time to play a deflection, when your prey is
less likely to be able to block it.

> We've always played that in order to react to a vampire's actions
> either by blocking or playing a different reaction card, you had
> to catch them doing it. The logic being that stealth represents
> your hiding what you're doing from sight, if they can't see you,
> how can they react at all to what you're doing.

It's not that I can't see you, its that I can't stop you.
I may have already given you misinformation that ends up
being the deflection / redirection / telepathic misdirection /
telepathic counter. Stealth isn't about not being seen, its
about not being blocked.

> Second question, if you have a directed bleed card, can you nominate
> someone besides your prey as the target?

Not unless the card mentions another player.
Bleeds are only directed at your prey unless the card
says specifically that you can bleed someone else.
See Cat Burglary, Night Moves, Kindred Spirits.
If any (D) bleed could target anyone, then these
cards would not need to exist. They do exist however
and are part of the argument that you may only bleed
your prey unless the card text says otherwise.

> We've always played that the built in bleed has to go to your prey,
> but a directed bleed can go to any methusulah. Otherwise, what is
> the card difference between a directed attack (say Ambush, which
> doesn't specify that it has to be your prey, just that it can't be
> your own minion) and a Computer Hacking, which doesn't say that it
> has to be directed at your prey either?

Ambush says "Enter combat with a tapped minion."
Any minion who is tapped (and not yours) can be targetted.

The (D) symbol only redundantly indicates who can block (only
the controller of the target, or the methuselah tragetted).
The symbol does *not* address who the action can be directed
at - the rest of the text on the card should make that clear.

All bleeds default to your prey, by the definition of "bleed".
See the online rulebook [6.1.1] here:

http://www.white-wolf.com/VTES/rulebook.html

"6.1.1. Bleed
Bleeding is one of the most fundamental actions of the game.
It is the basic means of removing your prey's pool. By default,
your minion's bleed actions can be directed only at your prey.
Some cards or effects may allow or force you to bleed a Methuselah
other than your prey. You can never bleed yourself, however."

This has not always been the case (if you ever called WOTC's
helpline, or emailed the newsgroup 2 or more years ago, they
would have told you otherwise), but has been the case since
July 7th, 1998 when the current Rules Team became official.

http://members.tripod.com/~Lasombra/RTR7-7.htm

Messages.Author: John Whelan
Messages.Body:
On Thu, 5 Oct 2000, Lee Fent wrote:

> If vampire A is bleeding at +1 Stealth (due to Kine Domination for
> example) can vampire B (controlled by the victim methusulah) play a
> deflection without generating +1 intercept?

Yes. Intercept is only for blocking. You don't need intercept to vote or
play reaction cards in political actions either.

If you needed intercept to play reaction cards, then you would never be
able to play the intercept cards in the first place.

> We've always played that
> in order to react to a vampire's actions either by blocking or playing
> a different reaction card, you had to catch them doing it. The logic
> being that stealth represents your hiding what you're doing from
> sight, if they can't see you, how can they react at all to what you're
> doing.

OK, but the rule being justified here is not an official rule. You can
just as easily use your imagination to justify the official rules.

> Second question, if you have a directed bleed card, can you nominate
> someone besides your prey as the target?

All bleeds are directed. The "directed" status of any action has nothing
to do with who may be targetted. It has to do with who can block. If an
action is directed, then only the targetted Methuselah can block. If an
action is non-directed, then only your predator and prey may block.

To determine who a bleed can be directed at, check the rulebook, or card
text, as appropriate. Most cards which are designated with the (D) symbol
(which just means "directed action", not "directed action which can target
anyone") will tell you who may be targetted. The exception are the bleed
cards. These do not tell you who may be targetted, because the rulebook
already tells you that bleeds are targetted at your prey.

The (D) symbol on bleed cards is simply reminder text, indicating that,
like all bleeds, this one is directed. This means that no-one may attempt
to block the action except the target. Political actions, by contrast,
are not directed actions (and so do not have the (D) symbol). Thus only
predator and prey may block such actions. You may not block them from
across the table, even if you feel the vote is victimizing you.

The only times bleeds can be directed at other than your prey is when card
text tells you this happens. Thus, deflection cards can send your bleed
to another Methuselah. Also, Cat Burglary, Night MOves, and Kindred
Spirits have card text that explicitly allow you to bleed other
Methuselahs.

> We've always played that the
> built in bleed has to go to your prey, but a directed bleed can go to
> any methusulah.

The distinction you are making is false. All bleeds are Directed
Actions. They are "directed" at your prey. That means only the target
(your prey) can block.

> Otherwise, what is the card difference between a
> directed attack (say Ambush, which doesn't specify that it has to be
> your prey, just that it can't be your own minion) and a Computer
> Hacking, which doesn't say that it has to be directed at your prey
> either?

There is no difference, as far as the significance of the (D) symbol goes.
In both cases, it means that only the targetted Methuselah may attempt to
block the action. In the case of Computer Hacking, the targetted
Methuselah is your prey (as per the rulebook on bleeds). In the case of
Ambush, the targetted Methuselah is whoever controls the tapped minion you
are trying to enter combat with.

> Sorry if these are stupid questions, but we've played with these as
> our interpretations for many years, and Norman gave us a wake up call,
> so now we're waking up, and like normal, we're a little bearish about
> it.

Actually, the confusion regarding the (D) symbol was long ago created and
spread by the original rules team. According to every rulebook ever
printed, the (D) symbol simply means "Directed Action" (which was fully
defined), but this did not stop the original rules team from ruling that
(D) meant "Directed Action that can target any Methuselah". This
confusing and pointless rule clearly ran counter to the design intent, and
was eventually eliminated by the current rules team. Now (D) means just
"Directed Action" again, which is as it should be.

-- John Whelan

Well, having read the replies, I have the following things to say.
Since they are not aimed at anyone in specific, I didn't reply to
anyone except my own post.

I think our problem is with the first part being an interpretation,
simply because it does NOT say that you can react without generating
the intercept first. In fairness it also does not say that you cannnot
react without the intercept. If you're only interested in
the "Official Ruling" stop reading here, I'll accept that any time I
leave this town I'll have to play by those rules, since they
are "Official". From here on out, I'm going to lay out my argument why
it shouldn't be that way.

Logically, not rules wise, since the rule book states that

"Conceptually, stealth represents the measures that the acting minion
is taking to conduct his business discreetly, to avoid attracting the
attention of those who would oppose him."

And that blocking is nothing more than a reaction to an action that, if
successful will end with combat instead of a more elegant solution
(deflection or reduction). I find it illogical to assume that you can
react to something that you cannot perceive. If you don't know that
I'm going to steal your money or wreck your business, or whatever the
bleed actually is representing, then how can you respond to it? And
that line about the methus being all seeing is fine, but he's still
giving directions to someone who can't see what's going on (the minion
attempting to react).

The interaction of voting is that you can't stop the vote from being
floored, but you can still respond by snarling and everything else to
the voting, not the calling of the vote.

Frankly I don't care if how we play isn't the official standpoint.
Sure, it's nice to play by the rules, but we play the game because of
the flavor. The official rules seem to be reducing the game to a
series of moves that are more mechanical than before. Fine, I won't
play any more with anyone outside who isn't willing to accept our house
rules. I really don't give a rats hindquarters about tournaments, I
have too many trophies from other games to care any more, and I don't
have the time or money to be competetive in V:TES too. It just seems
to me that with the official rules you really don't have to worry about
stealth bleed until you're down to two players, since you can deflect
it any time you want prior to that, you can rack up victory points
while your preditor puts out your prey for you. Gee, what a great
deal. I guess we play a harsher version here, since you can't deflect
it if you don't have the intercept to match. Since most bleeds start
at no stealth, you still have a chance to deflect, but the bleeds that
you're expending resources on (cards and blood) are more effective than
the built-in versions. Not because we can reduce it to a series of
actions that preordain a specific outcome. If I wanted to do that I'd
go back to playing Magic and winning every game. Before you say
anything take a moment to imagine a game where you have to generate the
intercept to stop a bleed, and you have to decide if you want to
deflect it before they play their bleed modifiers, which is the way we
play. The choices are harder, you have to know what you're doing
rather than waiting until after they play their modifiers to play your
reaction cards, and thus knowing before hand if it's better to take the
one bleed (you hope), waste the deflection on what might be a
insignificant bleed, or to honest to gosh block, and risk being unable
to stop them as the acting minion proves too wily for the blocking
minion.

Now if you want to flame me about this, fine, do it to me directly at
mailto://lf...@ionet.net (lf...@ionet.net for those without html
readers) rather than clog the ng with your bile. If someone ones to
discuss why these are not valid interpretations, fine, step up and have
a whack at it.

Thanks,
Lee

Yeah, those are hard choices - either you're screwed, or you're
screwed. Stealth decks beat intercept decks. It's a fact. Stealth
bleed will win every single game under your system, if constructed and
played properly. Decks don't have the resources available to generate
intercept, deflect, AND do something to their own prey.

>rather than waiting until after they play their modifiers to play your
>reaction cards, and thus knowing before hand if it's better to take the

>insignificant bleed, or to honest to gosh block, and risk being unable
>to stop them as the acting minion proves too wily for the blocking
>minion.

OK, look at this example, played under the official rules.

A comes to bleed B with his first of 3 minions, using Govern the
Unaligned. (bleed of 3).

B attempts to block.

A plays "Lost in Crowds" to add 2 stealth.

B says "OK, I fail miserably."

A now must ask himself "Is my prey going to Deflect this?" prior to
playing his Conditioning. He looks, and sees that the vampire B tried
to block with has superior Dominate and 3 blood on it - enough to pay
for a Deflection and stay untapped. Does B's attempt to block signal
that he has no Deflections, or was he trying to trick A into adding
stealth? If A guesses wrong, he will be helping his prey out by
bleeding his grandprey for 6 at 2 stealth. No easy task for A.

A doesn't play his Conditioning and says "No modifiers, only 3." (a
wise choice, since he can just play the Conditioning on the NEXT
bleed, and draw out 2 of B's Deflections at minimal risk).

B now must ask himself "Should I Deflect this?" Sure, it's a bleed
for 3, and that could hurt, but I only have one Deflection in hand,
and what happens if the next one is for 6? Does he have that many
bleed cards? Shit. Maybe he just doesn't have any modifiers, and
he'll have to bleed for 1 with his next two minions, so I'll end up
Deflecting a bleed for 1. Damn."

As you can see, there is no "gimme" for either player under the
official rules. If B has 3 Deflections in hand, of course, the choice
is much easier, but he was either very lucky, or a fool, since anyone
playing with THAT many Deflections to guarantee 3 in hand at all times
will be piteously helpless before a vote deck. If A gets greedy and
starts modifying every bleed, he certainly WILL oust his grandprey -
but if he sees potential Deflections, he can change his strategy some
to bleed for smaller amounts to force the Deflections out of his
prey's hand.

> We play that way. As long as the bleeding minion isn't at stealth you

This seems to go against your earlier justification of your house rule:

> Logically, not rules wise, since the rule book states that
>
> "Conceptually, stealth represents the measures that the acting minion
> is taking to conduct his business discreetly, to avoid attracting the
> attention of those who would oppose him."
>
> And that blocking is nothing more than a reaction to an action that, if
> successful will end with combat instead of a more elegant solution
> (deflection or reduction). I find it illogical to assume that you can
> react to something that you cannot perceive. If you don't know that
> I'm going to steal your money or wreck your business, or whatever the
> bleed actually is representing, then how can you respond to it?

You say you should have to catch him before you deflect him, but with
the latter, you don't allow him to evade.

If you have to catch to deflect, then logically it follows that if you
can deflect, you must've caught him. Which means that you should be
able to block if you are able to deflect. Which, as I understand it,
is not the way your house rule works - you can deflect even though if
you tried to block, you would fail (because the block attempt would
allow the actor to evade with stealth.

Intercepting an action (to block or, in your case, to deflect) is not
something you do just by playing intercept - it is a contest between
how much intercept you can generate and how much stealth the acting
minion can generate. As intercepting to block is not successful until
the acting minion "yields" (and chooses to add no more stealth), so
should your rule of intercepting to deflect.

Incidentally, what is the nature/source of your house rule's distinction
between say, inferior and superior Telepathic Misdirection. One you can
play even when the minion doesn't "perceive" the action, the other you
cannot (by your house rule).

Our house rules work like this.
Minion A comes to bleed at no stealth. Minion B can choose to react or
not. If they Deflect then Minion A is bleeding someone else, who then
has a chance to react or not. Since no one has tried to block Minion
A, he is still at no stealth. If instead of deflecting or countering
Minion B chooses to Block, then minion A can attempt to evade by
increasing stealth. Minion B and Minion A then trade back and forth
until either Minion A has no more stealth, or Minion B has no more
intercept.

If Minion A used Kine Dominnace (Directed Bleed at +1 Bleed +1 Stealth)
then Minion B would have to generate an intercept before he could
deflect or attempt to block. After generating the inital +1 intercept,
things pretty much follow as above.

In order to be valid to block/deflect/react, you must match Minion A's
stealth. I think I'm not doing a very good job of explaining this.
Basically you have to be able to intercept someone (generate at least
enough intercept to see the action) before you can choose how you want
to respond. How you respond is up to your choice and the cards.
Another thing we do is that you don't add Action Modifiers until the
window for reaction is past. Meaning that you've past by their
deflecting/countering/blocking period when you play Threats or anything
else (except superiour Bonding and other Stealth cards). Norman chose
to deflect after modifiers were played, which by our table is a serious
no-no. By that time in the evening it was late and we were all a
little razzled, so I chose not to mention it. Several other snafu's
occured that we chose not to get into since it wasn't worth it to
disrupt the game further than it already had been. Anyway, hope that
explain how our system works.

Lee

I guess that most people on the newsgroup are going to say that they prefer to
have one method of defense against bleeding...they don't want to have to guess
about how/whether or not they're going to defend against a bleed. I think
that it's unlikely that any [competitive | working] deck could pack enough
deflections to deflect *every* bleed by a S&B deck...the reason they're in
there is to keep the predator honest. Any given S&B deck can simply slow down
to a Govern the Unaligned per vampire, no modifiers, and that's still pretty
painful. Using deflections puts the burden of "guessing" on the predator.
"Is he going to deflect this one and oust *his* prey, or am I going to get it
through?"

In short, S&B is *very* powerful, except when it runs up against combat.
Deflection is one of a few possible defenses against it. Every other style of
deck has multiple avenues of defense (oooh...just turned the old "avenues of
attack" on it's head...I think I'm in trouble for that malapropism...), so why
should S&B have *just* Rush combat and Intercept be its counters? Rush
combat, while *awesome* isn't...defensive enough for some people. I guess
they don't like having to wait around until their turn to do stuff.

playing an S&B deck. Legbiter said elsewhere (in a sentence I think was a
little convoluted) that it's not deflection that kills S&B, but Rush combat
keeps people from playing S&B much.

That's all...

Tim,
Well, let me see if I can explain how our deviant system works, since
this seems to be what most people are stumbling over. (How on earth it
worked at all I mean)

1) We follow the no multiples for action mods/reactions, and no repeat
actions (although this is a recent addition).
2) Telepathic Misd is harder, but only in the sense that it might
require another auspex card, just like Deflection might require one.
3) Dread Gaze and such are played in the "After the action is
successful" state (our sequencing differs from the normal too). The
vote has been called, during the voting is when they kick in. If you
Delay, the vote is returned to your hand etc etc...

Generally we have a mix of decks, someone almost always brings a combat
deck, and someone usually has a "theme" deck. The rest are
usually "theory" decks and such. S&B is currently out of favor since
there is nearly always a cbt deck at hand.

Well, new players are always welcome, and until Wed night, we never had
anyone play any other way, so that was the first time. Since only two
other people where there, it's hard to say what the reaction will be.
It happened that it was two of the major players, and both of them hold
much sway in the way things are done, so maybe things will change.

I come from a competitive magic back ground, I rarely go past 62 cards,
and more than 4CL is a "weird-out" moment for me. I'm working at it,
but it's not easy, and some people are more helpful than others. In
the past we had a hard 4CL, but since we now realize that we have a
limited card pool that everyone is pulling from, it's hard to go more
than 4 without harming someone else's deck. Since we play for fun,
it's generally not done unless you really feel that you have to have 4
or more of whatever card...

Thanks for listening.

Lee

never had a problem with collusion. It's a risk we all run. If you'd
say, just for example, played Fame on Fredrick, then I might seek to do
you harm because of that. Not to the point that I allow your prey to
take you out, but rather in the form of "persuading" you to not do that
anymore. Since we have a stable group equilibrium, we don't have
collusion problems. Our problems usually come in the form of cross
game grudges, where when you beat all of my vampires into torpor in one

agreement, and I'm not doing it to help your predator out, I don't
think of it as collusion. It's the way it's been here for the longest
time.

Well, since most people here (perhaps not so in the future) have been
brought into a standing game where there are multiple people who play
by the rules, and since they usually learn by playing a few hands with
everyone helping them, there usually isn't a big moment of shock
involved. I think it is enough for new players to learn a complicated
game... but then of course, my copy of the V:TES Official
Clarifications, Rulings, and Errata is just over 1800 lines long. We
try not to introduce all the rules at once, but to do them in slow
little chunks. If there is a new player, no one pulls fancy stuff, we
stick to simple decks (demo style decks I mean) and play in a friendly
game. We don't attack people for no reason, we don't block hunting, or
other "rude" things. We try to point out where and when something can
be done so that the player is aware of the potentials.

A comes to bleed B with his first of 3 minions, using Govern the

Actually, I am rather enjoying this tete a'tete. If you would like
commentary. I will comment that you two have gone way past the
intercept plus reaction vs. just-reaction card debate, and into some
twilight zone of stealth bleed nastiness.

The truth of the matter is that if you cannot play deflections unless
you have enough intercept to block, then you have zero chance of winning
if someone shows up with dedicated stealth bleed. As defense no longer
works, then speed becomes the only factor in the game. Therefore large
vampires can no longer be played with any reasonable strength, as there
is guaranteed to be intercept on the table to try (and fail) to create
defenses. So now 5th trads and Minion taps only work for the Nossies
and the Malks. So now, you have to play with intercept in your deck
because there is no other defense (except for vote defense, which is
handled in an illogical manner under your intercept to play reaction
cards except for vote reactions).

So now you can't really play with a toned deck if you want to play
defense, because you have to water it down with intercept. And all you
do with all that intercept is just jam up on it as it clogs your hand,
if there isn't mass amounts of stealth around. So now to Deflect or
Telepathically Counter any of your bleeds, I have to generate enough
intercept but if I cannot then these cards jam my hand up. So now to
counter a S+B deck I have to either be preyed on by them or hopelessly
jam up on all the intercept that I have in my hand. So if my predator
is a Stealth-Bleeder, the first thing he does is flush all the defense
out of your hand, then hit you with the Conditionings, or if my
predator is not a Stealth-Bleeder then he comes at you and you jam on
all the intercept that you were going to use against a stealth bleeder.

All of this has already been said, but, unfortunantly, specific counter
examples have been brought up that only address the individual
situations rather that the game altering mechanism of reactions
requiring intercept to play them.

Comments Welcome,

Batter Up!

[SNIP]

> I ignore it, oust my prey, and move on. Weenie voters move quick,
> yes, but so do I, and a weenie vote deck is more of a threat to the
> table than my S&B - so don't expect your predator to leave YOU alone

Sorry, in the model I imagined, I am your prey. I was talking about my
way of dealing with your S&B. I'm also not so certain about the table
fearing me more than you. Light intercept hoses me, very little hoses
your "tuned" deck. Very few moving parts and whatnot. I think those
were your statements. Who are you afraid of now? I think the tables I
play at would support the weenie votes, since during the time that I'm
taking you out, they're slowly moving towards their voters, and
weakening me all that much more. It may very well be a war of mutual
ousting since I may defeat you only to find that I lack to voting power
to roll over anyone else.

[SNIP]

> KRCs. If you want to Dramatic Upheaval in front of me, fine. The
> table will be on MY side if you try to Dramatic Upheaval with me and
> steal my prey, since a vote deck that does that is more of a threat
> than a bleed deck. With a weenie vote deck, you won't be Parity
> Shifting me since you'll have more pool (spent less for vampires).
> Banishment is mildly annoying, but not a major crisis.

I think banishment may be a little more effective than you give it
credit for. First, it halts a vampire of yours for a complete turn
(from my vote to your influence), if you've been using that vampire to
Govern or whatever, then it's possible that you won't get the vampire
up for more than a round. Which is a major loss of firepower when I
banish a vampire or two (1/3 to 2/3's of your minions). With S&B,
every round counts, it is a fairly speed intensive deck, so a halt of
even a round may be fatal for the deck.

> About the best thing you can do to affect me is drop KRC after KRC
> after KRC and try to do as much damage as I can.

I don't have to do as much, I'm on weenies remember. But still the
point is valid, I must equal or out accelerate you, otherwise the
damage you can deal out will overwhelm the buffer that a weenie deck
provides. However, what does this have to do with whether or not
intercept before catching at stealth actions is a playable house rule?

[SNIP]

> Both. I was manipulating my opponents to a small degree with
> deal-making, and I was making the ABSOLUTE BEST use of what my deck
> had provided to me at that point in time. Was it deck-building skill?
> No. Was it just good play? yes. It almost looks like you agree, in
> your last sentence: my point is that play skill is MUCH more
> important than deck-building.

I can agree that Play skill is valuable, but I don't agree that it
is "MUCH more important". By that logic, I can take a poorly
constructed deck, hand them to a Great player and expect to see them
perform well (not strictly win or oust). You've got to have a deck
that can win before any degree of skill matters. Have you ever
accidentally switched your crypt with another deck of yours, and then
sat down to play? That's what a badly constructed deck performs like.

> Wow, that's a horrible, horrible idea. If your hand is "good", why
> would you want to use any of the cards in it to no purpose?

How about I guess at this one. If your hand is good, shouldn't you be
doing something with it? I don't think it's a horrible idea, it is an
idea that varies wildly with the deck that you're playing. A defender
deck or one that is waiting to see if there are deflections shouldn't
burn cards aimlessly, but a rush deck or a vote deck is burning them
like crazy being active as all get out. Different decks, different
modes of play.

> I've seen people lose a game they should've won by trying to
> frantically use up cards in their hand without a good reason to do so.
> Just because you have the bleed cards in your hand doesn't mean you
> should bleed for more than 1. And just because you have the
> Conditioning in your hand doesn't mean you should drop it on the first
> bleed.

Umm, okay. I shall now meditate on the Tao of card games....

[Yanked the math section since I don't think that either of us should
be arguing about it considering there is strong chance that we don't
know what we are talking about, and there is a very bad potential for
some seriously OT discussion about probability mathematics.]

prevents me from rushing back, or voting damage to you for your little
bleed retaliation. I think the reason we don't have any deals is that
several of us are friends, and it pretty much sucks to sit down and get
beat by a cluster of people playing hard with you, but nice with each
other. I mean when Norman visited, he sat down against two guys that
have been friends their entire lives. He probably wouldn't have
enjoyed having his ass beaten by two decks at one. Which, by our
misinterpretation of the directed bleed rule, would have easily been
allowed.

[SNIP]

>

Which is a SM that isn't going to bother me. The fact that you bled

> AGAIN, the "anti-X" comes in. You keep bringing the Rush deck up. If

Fine, replace the words "rush his 4 blood into torpor" with Banish
Ozmo/Roland/Didi/Whomever, is that better for you? Do I really need to
list all the ways to neutralize a vampire everytime? If so I'm just
gonna make a standard disclaimer and paste it in every time. Ugh.

Well, like you enjoy pointing out to me. You have one deflection, your

doing more than one bounce per round (Didi), so you can stop 1 of 1

desire to tangle up vampires in combat and risk them anyway, and to

leave a vampire untapped just to deflect or block. Ya know, I sorta
like using your arguements against you, makes me feel all tingly. :P

[SNIP]

> Who cares? =) If Ohanna bleeds you for 8 over 2 turns, someone can

> it's not Ohanna doing this in our example above, but the point still
> stands - 8 pool damage from a 2 pool cost vampire is what we like to

Given, but she didn't get through in speed mode, she can't go to
stealth without help. But with timing and some patience, I'll give it

Is that the one that you have posted on the website? Please. Light
intercept stops it dead since it can't govern effectively anymore, and
bonding isn't that spectacular. You know that, what was the point of
this?

> Um, the only time a vampire's blood matters is when it has 0, and has
> to hunt. Thinking that the first 2 blood off of Didi Myers is a "40%
> reduction in strength" is a VERY inaccurate assumption. In fact, it

Actually it is a precisely accurate statement. She is in fact at 40%
of her max. Her ability to attack is unblemished, so in your speed
S&B, she is just as useful to you until she reaches a lower point, but
for blocking/deflecting she's rapidly loosing her ability to cope.

[SNIP]

> I've heard about a deck that uses Info Highway to drag out multiple
> Inner Circle members, who he then Minion Taps down to 2 blood and then
> uses very few discipline cards that cost blood - and if they run out
> of blood, they just hunt! His theory is "Who cares? It's 4 votes, +2
> bleed, and it cost me 2 pool, a Minion Tap, and 2 turns of transfers."
> It's not foolproof, of course, but it's certainly not a BAD approach -
> since again, that's over 80% of the blood removed from an IC member,
> and they're still at 100% offensive strength.

I have a deck called big-guns, a counter to certain unfounded claims
that I can only build weenie decks. It functions along very similar
lines, using Govern/Scouting/Enchant Kindred to add blood to it's
younger members, and minion taps to bring that back in. The deck
performs amazingly well since I intended to lose with it, so every win
is a shocker to me.

very hesitant to aid/abet a weenie vote deck in any form. Also, more
people pack bounce than intercept - so in the situation you describe,
the table is likely to look at you as "pool soak", and get on with the
business of getting their own VPs while the two of us beat each other
up.

If you turn to the right, it DOES become an individual duel and you
have an advantage since your prey is ignoring you, while your predator
is attempting to oust me. But if you do this, then you will not gain
any VPs yourself, as you -will- be rolled over by my predator, and
your prey will have built up plenty of defense. Whereas, if you moved
forward as fast as possible, you could potentially gain a VP before I
ousted you, which would really damage my OWN chances - as the S&B's
whole idea is "move really fast".

reasonably effective counter to any strategy based on bleeding, and

some of the library cards... and swept the table. An unopened box of
starters qualifies as "poorly constructed deck", to me. It sure as
hell ain't a natural table-sweeper, and it probably can't do any given
trick more than once.

The value that play skill adds is much more than you think.

(Switching crypts with another deck isn't poorly constructed, it's
simply UNPLAYABLE since you can't use any of your cards. If I swapped

You're not seven times more likely, since there's a possibility you
might draw more than one in your draw, which is -- for the purposes of
this probability discussion -- equivalent to drawing just one.

I went and dug through some references to find the paragraph this whole
discussion refers to.

>I didn't use at least 1 and usually 2+ card up during my turn. Giving
>me 4 chances to replace that used deflection, which is a 40% (assuming
>8 deflections in a 80 card deck) Some of the above comments can be

Let's assume that you have, indeed, played or discarded four cards
during your turn, one of which was a Deflection. You will now be
replacing four cards from a deck of 73 (80 cards - a 7 card hand)
containing 7 Deflections.

For each card you draw, the chance of it NOT being a Deflection is equal
to the number of cards left in the deck that are not Deflections divided
by the total number of cards in the deck.

Thus, the chance of you NOT getting a Deflection in four draws is:

66/73 * 65/72 * 64/71 * 63/70 = .662

Therefore, the chance of you getting at least one is 1 - .662 = .338 =
34%.
